1:
Ellicott sets out the chapter's architecture before anything else: three cases of instigation to idolatry are considered, the false prophet, the private individual and the city, and in every case the penalty is the same, death without mercy. He then meets the suggestion that so severe a law must be the production of a later age, granting that it may have been more often broken than observed but pointing to episodes in the history which seem to require some such law in all three of its sections, since the case of the false prophet is what justifies Elijah in taking the prophets of Baal down to the brook Kishon. Calvin explains why the warning was needed at this point: having restrained them from the delusions of the surrounding nations, the lawgiver now guards against false teachers arising from among themselves, since peril is to be feared not only from professed enemies but because Satan plots by intestine deceits and abuses the holy name of God to betray us. From that Calvin draws his rule, that the faith of the godly must not only be fortified externally by the ramparts of the word against corruption creeping in from without, but garrisoned within by the same word lest novel imaginations secretly insinuate themselves.

Henry finds the supposition strange twice over. It is strange that any should arise from among themselves, and especially any pretending to vision and prophecy, who should instigate them to serve other gods, since it seems hardly possible that a man with knowledge enough to personate a prophet should have so little knowledge of the divine nature as to go after other gods himself; and yet, Henry adds, we see it in our own day, multitudes professing both learning and religion while exciting others to worship God by images and to give divine honour to saints and angels, such is the power of strong delusions. Stranger still, he says, is that the sign given to confirm the false doctrine should actually come to pass. Gill answers the second difficulty by naming the possible means, that the wonder is performed or seemingly performed by sleight of hand, by magic art, or by the help of the devil, and permitted for the trial of the faith of God's people and the hardening of others. Clarke lists what the two words for sign and wonder may cover, from an apparently miraculous proof of mission to a type or representation of the thing the prophet wants them brought over to, and instances images pretended to have fallen from heaven.

What it means that the Lord proveth you raises a question about divine knowledge, and Calvin answers it by rejecting a famous solution. The verb, he says, when applied to God is never used in a bad sense of taking by guile or laying snares for the unwary, but only of proving or examining; God proves men's hearts not that he may learn what was before unknown but to lay open what was concealed, so that the expression to know refers to experimental knowledge only. He then quotes Augustine's version of the point, that God permits us to be tempted not that he may know, from whom nothing is hidden, but that he may cause us to know how far we have advanced in his love, and calls it tame and involved: since human feelings are so commonly attributed to God, there is no use twisting words which signify no more than that God makes trial so that what might otherwise be doubtful is displayed. Keil and Delitzsch draw a different conclusion from the same verse, that however great the importance attached to signs and wonders they were not to be regarded in Israel as the highest test or as absolutely decisive. Clarke makes experience the safeguard, since one who knows God experimentally cannot be drawn away.
4:
Keil and Delitzsch fix who is being commanded before anything else. The execution of seducers to idolatry is enjoined upon the people, that is upon the whole community and not upon single individuals, but specifically upon the authorities who had to maintain and administer justice; and the verb rendered thrust means to force thee from the way in which the Lord has commanded thee to walk. They note that the neuter in the closing formula about putting the evil away is settled by comparison with a later chapter. Wesley reads the same verb as marking the great force and power of seducers to corrupt men's minds, and glosses the formula tersely: thou shalt remove the guilt by removing the guilty. Gill takes the walking after the Lord as covering moral conduct, civil conduct and religious worship alike, citing the Targum for walking after the worship of the Lord, and reports from the same source that the death intended was by the sword. Calvin explains why the sentence follows where it does, that having already warned them not to listen to all teachers indifferently but to distinguish true from false and give credit only after judgement, the lawgiver now adds the punishment of those who creep in under the name of a prophet.

Calvin is careful to limit the severity twice over before defending it. He does not condemn to capital punishment those who may have spread false doctrine on account of some particular or trifling error, but only those who are the authors of apostasy and pluck up religion by the roots, which is why the gross form of the impiety is expressly named as trying to turn the people from the worship of the true God. And the season of such severity, he says, would not arrive until a positive religion had been established: the crime of impiety would not otherwise merit punishment unless the religion had been received by public consent and the suffrages of the people, and were supported besides by sure and indisputable proofs placing its truth beyond doubt. From that he draws a two-edged conclusion, that while the severity of those who defend superstitions with the sword is preposterous, yet in a well constituted polity profane men by whom religion is subverted are by no means to be tolerated. He adds that all excuse had been obviated in this case, since it was sufficiently manifest who God is and how he is to be worshipped, both by the wonderful blessing of the redemption from Egypt and by the doctrine of the law.

The argument Calvin then mounts runs from the lesser offence to the greater, and it is put with heat. Those who call such teaching sanguinary are, he says, unable to endure any restraint on their liberty to make disturbances; and to the objection that the truth of God stands in no need of such support he answers that this is very true, but asks what madness it is to impose a law on God that he should not use the obedience of magistrates in the matter, since God could indeed defend religion without the sword but such is not his will. Then the comparisons: in minor offences the judge may not hesitate, yet when the worship of God is violated shall so great a crime be fostered by his dissimulation; capital punishment is decreed against adulterers, yet shall the despisers of God adulterate the doctrines of salvation with impunity; pardon is never extended to poisoners, by whom the body alone is harmed. The note printed with Calvin observes that the principle laid down here is in effect his final apology for his part in the death of Servetus, and appends a modern historian's four points in his defence, among them that the matter was adjudicated by the magistrates of Geneva rather than by Calvin.
6:
Henry reads the list of relations as a study in the tempter's method. It is his policy to send his solicitations by the hand of those we love, whom we least suspect of a bad design and are most desirous to please, so that the enticement comes from a brother or child near by nature and a wife or friend near by choice; and Henry instances the tempting of Adam by Eve and of Christ by Peter, drawing the caution that we must guard against a bad proposal precisely when the person making it can plead an interest in us. He notes too that the temptation is supposed to be private, which implies that idolatry is a work of darkness dreading the light. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase about the son of thy mother not as marking a half-brother but as bringing out the closeness of the fraternal relation, matching it with the wife of thy bosom who rests upon thy breast and the friend who is as thine own soul, meaning one loved as much as life. Calvin explains why the same penalty reaches a private person, that although his ignorance is more excusable and no office increases his responsibility, apostasy is intolerable to God from whatever quarter it arises.

The evidentiary difficulty is Gill's contribution, and he takes it seriously. The offender was not to be killed privately where the enticement happened, nor by the enticed on his own authority, but only after examination and sentence by the civil magistrate, and no one might judge a false prophet but the great council at Jerusalem. But how could the case be proved, when the affair was transacted secretly with none present but the two parties, so that either the enticer must confess or the testimony of the enticed alone be taken? Gill reports the rabbinic answer: they laid wait for the enticer, which they never did for any other offender, the enticed bringing two persons and setting them behind a hedge where they could see and hear him without being seen, and then saying, say to me again privately what thou hast said. Ellicott finds a different safeguard in the requirement that the witness strike first, since where a witness must himself carry out or help carry out the sentence he demands, secret accusation becomes impossible and it is far less easy to pervert the law to prosecute a private quarrel. Calvin gives the same reason, that God would have those who denounced the crime be the executors of its punishment so that they should be more cautious in testifying.

On the reason annexed to the sentence Calvin hears an aggravation drawn from ingratitude. The clause about him who brought thee out of Egypt exaggerates the crime in proportion to the inestimable blessing of the deliverance, since it was gross wickedness to rebel against God after knowing him but grosser still to undervalue the Deliverer. He then names the fruit of the severity, that while punishment fell on one man's crime all others were inspired with terror, so that the death of one becomes a wholesome discipline for all by way of example. Keil and Delitzsch quote that very phrase back and then guard it: the fear of punishment given here as the end of the punishment is not the principle lying at the foundation of the law, but simply, as Calvin expresses it, the utility and fruit of severity, one reason for carrying it out and not to be confounded with the deterrent theory. Ellicott traces the law's later operation, holding that it justifies Jehu and Jehoiada in destroying Baal and accounts for the covenant made under Asa, and adds that though it may seem harsh its principle reappears in the gospel sayings about loving father or mother more than Christ.
12:
Henry marks two limits on the third case before it is described. The crime is supposed to be committed by one of the cities of Israel, lying within the jurisdiction of their own courts, since the church judged only those within; those born within a prince's allegiance who take up arms are dealt with as traitors while foreign invaders are not. And the city supposed is one that formerly worshipped the true God and has now withdrawn to others, which shows how great the crime is and how sore the punishment of those who turn aside after they have known the way of righteousness. Ellicott finds only one instance of the case in the history, that of Gibeah, and argues it fairly: the abominations done there may be assumed connected with idolatry from later allusions, though it was the outrage rather than the idolatry that roused Israel, and he notes that the remonstrance with the Benjamites seems to echo the language of this very chapter in asking that the men be delivered up and evil put away from Israel. Keil and Delitzsch correct the construction, since the preposition never means of one, so that the sense is not hearing in one city about another but simply hearing that in one of thy cities worthless men have risen up.

The name given to the instigators is worked over by four of them. Clarke derives it from two words meaning not and profit, cites the Greek version for lawless men, and glosses it as persons good for nothing to themselves or others and capable of nothing but mischief. Gill offers the same two possibilities, either men without a yoke who have thrown off the law and will not submit, or unprofitable men who are of no use to God, themselves or anyone. Calvin sets out the grammatical grounds for both readings, that if the vowel points are conceded the word is compounded so as to mean one thing while if they are disregarded it may be read as insubmissive or rebellious, and then declares the second opinion the more correct, that these are men of nothing in whom nothing good or praiseworthy is found. Ellicott reports that modern scholars generally explain it as worthlessness, notes that this is the first place the expression occurs with a passage in Judges the second, and records that Rashi curiously makes it destroyers of the yoke. Calvin adds the observation that gives the phrase its point here, that men do not all break into impiety at the same moment but Satan stirs up some who act as fans to excite the rest.

The inquiry commanded before any action is where Gill supplies the fullest detail, reporting the rabbinic procedure as a sequence. The case fell only to the great council at Jerusalem, which sent and inquired until it knew clearly that the whole city or the greater part was turned to idolatry; two disciples of the wise were then sent to admonish them, and if they repented it was well, but if they continued the council ordered all Israel up against them, besieging the city until it was broken up, after which many courts were set up to judge the inhabitants one by one on the testimony of two witnesses. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same requirement in its own terms, that the people as a whole, through their rulers, were to examine closely whether the thing was founded in truth, and note that the phrase about all that is in it relates to men, cattle and material property alike rather than to men only. Calvin infers the atrocity of the crime from the scale of the sentence, since the severity of a just and moderate ruler in a sedition does not usually go beyond punishing the ringleaders, whereas here all without exception are commanded to be destroyed.
15:
Who exactly falls under the sentence is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, and the two who address it directly take opposite views. Wesley restricts the word for the inhabitants to those who are guilty and not the innocent part, meaning such as disowned the apostasy, who he thinks would doubtless have left so wicked a place by their own choice or at least upon warning; and he explains the destruction by a parallel, that it is the punishment inflicted on the cities of the Canaanites, to whom having made themselves equal in sin it is just that God should equal them in punishment. Calvin faces the harder form of the objection and does not soften it: if any should say that the little children at least were innocent, his answer is that since all are condemned by the judgment of God from the least to the greatest, we contend against him in vain. He gives his reason for thinking the error unpardonable in the adults, that its authors were educated in the law and could not be deceived involuntarily unless they had grown weary of religion, and cites Jeremiah sending the people to distant isles to ask whether any nation has changed its gods.

On the burning of the spoil Calvin distinguishes two possible reasons and prefers one. It might be that the intention was to obviate covetousness, lest zeal be mixed up with rapine; but the principal reason is the one the text gives, that the people might be more accustomed to detest a crime they saw so cruelly punished. He presses the Hebrew word, which properly means destruction or abolition, and notes that what God would have annihilated because he cannot bear the sight of it is so called before him, which is why the phrase should be rendered thou shalt burn it to the Lord thy God rather than for him. Clarke draws a consequence from the same prohibition that none of the others reach: since they were not permitted to take the spoils of these cities, they could be under no temptation to make war on them, the thing being possible only from a religious motive since no profit could come of it — and he adds the reflection that few religious wars would ever have been fought had they been regulated by the principle that one may neither extend territory nor take spoil. Gill reports the rabbinic detail that if a city had no street they made one, and Wesley that the ruin was to stand as an eternal monument.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the promise of mercy and increase is attached to the command about the accursed thing. Nothing whatever was to remain hanging to the hand of Israel, so that the Lord might turn from his wrath and have compassion on the nation, that is not punish the sin of one town upon the whole people but multiply it, making up the diminution consequent on the destruction of that town's inhabitants and so fulfilling the promise given to the fathers about the multiplying of their seed. Wesley states the same in a sentence, that they should have no loss of their numbers by cutting off so many people. Gill explains what cleaving to the hand would have meant by pointing to Achan, since all being devoted to destruction was cursed and would bring a curse on whoever made it his own property. Ellicott hears an echo of this verse in the close of that story, where all Israel stoned him and raised a great heap of stones and the Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger; he also matches the burning of the city and its cattle to the treatment of Gibeah. Clarke notes simply that the contagion had to be destroyed in its birth.
